4.2.4. The lower court identified a further violation of the non-compete clause in the fact that, 
unlike in the client letter, the expert letter stated that Arkadium AG acted “as a leading 
headhunter in the Construction & Property sector serving as a source of information for the 
experts,” and further: “Arkadium specializes in the Construction and Property sector and focuses 
exclusively on the following areas: Architecture, civil engineering, construction logistics, 
building services engineering, the energy sector, property, asset and real estate management, lean 
construction, and digitalization.”  
The statement immediately preceding this—namely, that the plaintiff’s operational business 
would be taken over by Arkadium—already creates the impression that Arkadium alone is now 
responsible for the candidates. The following sentence reinforces this impression, especially 
since it suggests that one can feel secure with Arkadium as a “leading headhunter.” Even the one-
time use of this sentence constitutes an abusive advertising practice, particularly since the 
statement “leading headhunter” has a striking effect. Even the defendant did not dispute that he 
or Arkadium had used it to promote themselves. Furthermore, the statement follows a list of 
straightforward facts about “client processes,” “ongoing assignments,” “client management,” and 
“placement processes with candidates.” As such, it stands out. This advertisement clearly goes 
beyond what would have been necessary to inform the candidates (experts). Therefore, the 
defendant was not permitted to use any names, trademarks, or parts of the plaintiff’s name in this 
advertising. Whether the content of the advertising was accurate is irrelevant.  
Finally, the lower court identified a third violation of the non-competition clause but disregarded 
it because the plaintiff had not raised an objection to it. 
4.2.5. With regard to the alleged violations of the non-competition clause, the lower court further 
considered that the defendant had not proven that he was not at fault. Moreover, given his 
business experience, it was evident that he had acted with at least conditional intent in drafting 
and sending the expert letter. This is also supported by the fact that he apparently took the trouble 
to specifically adapt the expert letter as compared to the client letter.
